name: D-mannose (by mouth)
short: Case report: serum sickness-like reaction in a 16-year-old on a D-mannose supplement, recurring on restart. Pregnancy, one woman with a rare disorder: baby growth-restricted. Trials: few, mild events.
text: A case report describes a serum sickness-like reaction, an immune reaction with rash, joint pain and fever, in a 16-year-old girl taking a supplement whose active ingredient the abstract gives as D-mannose, alongside other medicines: she developed a widespread hives-like rash, headaches, joint pain and swelling, she was treated with prednisone and antihistamines and all her medicines were stopped, her symptoms resolved, and restarting the supplement triggered a recurrence; the abstract does not list the supplement's other ingredients. A 2022 Cochrane review of 7 trials of D-mannose for preventing or treating urinary tract infections (719 adult women and men) found adverse events very few and poorly reported, none serious, mostly diarrhoea and vaginal burning. In a trial of 308 women, 17.9% of those in the D-mannose and nitrofurantoin groups reported side effects, which were mild and did not require stopping, with a significantly lower risk of side effects with D-mannose than with nitrofurantoin; a 2020 review reports diarrhoea in 8 of 103 women given D-mannose alone in one study and none in another of 10. A 2025 meta-analysis of 4 trials in 890 adult women found that adverse events did not differ significantly between D-mannose and placebo or no treatment (risk ratio 2.19, 95% CI 0.68 to 7.05, with high heterogeneity). The abstract of the largest placebo-controlled trial, in 598 women, gives no adverse-event data. In a randomised trial in postmenopausal women who stayed on vaginal oestrogen (57 enrolled, 32 completed), D-mannose was well tolerated with high adherence; the abstract gives no event counts. With proanthocyanidins and other ingredients in one combined supplement, a trial reports a low incidence of side effects, with diarrhoea the most frequent in both groups. Pregnancy: in a woman with MPI-CDG, a rare inherited disorder treated with oral D-mannose, the doctors stopped it at 6 weeks of pregnancy because of potential fetal toxicity seen particularly in animal models, then restarted it at 10 weeks when her symptoms returned; human data on birth defects are lacking, growth restriction of the baby was noted before delivery at 38 weeks, and the baby had a low Apgar score but recovered quickly. In 8 people with this disorder given oral D-mannose for a median of almost 15 years, two developed severe portal hypertension, two venous thrombosis and one altered kidney function; the abstract does not attribute these to D-mannose and links poor compliance to recurrence of thrombosis, and the pregnancy report describes the disorder itself as causing impaired coagulation and liver disease. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
